entry.title: Does Your Company Really Need Kubernetes? Or Are You Just Cosplaying as Netflix?
entry.summary: Kubernetes is brilliant technology, but most small teams don't need it. What premature infrastructure really costs, what to run instead, and when to switch.
entry.content:
Everyone wants Kubernetes.

The DevOps engineer wants it. The CTO read about it. The founder saw a company using it and thought, "We should probably do that too."

Suddenly a company with three developers, one API and a PostgreSQL database is planning a Kubernetes migration.

For what? Millions of requests? Hundreds of microservices? Multiple regions?

No. Because Kubernetes is what serious engineering teams use.

Right?

Wrong.

This is one of the most expensive mistakes in modern software engineering: confusing infrastructure complexity with engineering maturity.

Great technology, wrong problem

Kubernetes is an incredible piece of technology. It orchestrates containers. It manages workloads across clusters. It handles service discovery, scaling and self-healing. It solves real problems. Big ones.

But here's the part the shiny architecture diagrams leave out: Kubernetes doesn't eliminate complexity. It moves it somewhere else. And sometimes it creates more of it.

The migration nobody can justify

Say you're building a SaaS product. You have an API, a background worker, a PostgreSQL database and maybe Redis for caching. You serve a few thousand customers. Deployments are straightforward. The cloud bill is manageable. When something breaks, the team knows where to look.

Life is good.

Then someone says, "We should move to Kubernetes."

Why?

"Scalability."

What does that mean?

"We need to be ready for growth."

How much growth?

Silence.

What exactly is the current system failing to do?

More silence.

The migration begins anyway. Now the team needs to understand pods, deployments, services, ingress controllers, ConfigMaps, Secrets, persistent volumes, resource requests and limits, liveness probes, readiness probes and cluster networking. That's before anyone debugs why one service can't reach another at 2 am.

Congratulations. You just turned a simple deployment into a distributed infrastructure problem.

And your customers? They still see the same login page. The same dashboard. The same API. Nothing changed for them. Your team just has more to maintain, more to monitor, more that can fail and more that needs specialist knowledge. All for a scaling problem you haven't actually had.

That's what optimising for imaginary problems instead of real ones looks like. I've made the same argument about microservices, and it applies here for the same reasons.

Kubernetes isn't the villain

Let's be fair. The villain is premature complexity. There's a difference.

Kubernetes can be an excellent choice when:

  • You run dozens of services across multiple teams.
  • Your deployment requirements are genuinely complex.
  • Your workloads really benefit from orchestration.
  • An infrastructure team needs consistent deployment patterns across many applications.
  • Your organisation has the operational expertise to run it properly.

A five-person startup shipping an MVP is none of those. It's solving the wrong problem.

Here's the uncomfortable truth: your company probably doesn't need more infrastructure. It needs more customers. Product-market fit. Faster feedback loops. Better onboarding. Fewer bugs. A product people will pay for.

Nobody has ever bought your SaaS because you used Kubernetes. Nobody woke up this morning thinking, "I'd love to use this project management tool, but I'm not convinced their containers are orchestrated properly."

Customers care whether the product works. Whether it's fast enough. Whether it solves their problem. Whether they can trust it.

That's it. If a simpler platform delivers those outcomes, why add another layer to operate?

You don't install Kubernetes. You operate it.

This is the hidden cost. Someone has to understand how it works, configure it securely, monitor it, upgrade it and investigate its incidents. Someone has to manage networking, resource allocation, failed deployments and the growing pile of YAML nobody wants to touch.

If you don't have those people, your application developers become your infrastructure team. Instead of building features, they debug the cluster. Instead of talking to customers, they chase failed deployments. Instead of improving the product, they learn why a workload keeps restarting.

Sometimes that's a worthwhile investment. Often it's an expensive distraction. The difference is whether the infrastructure solves a problem that matters to the business.

Every technology choice has an opportunity cost. Time spent maintaining infrastructure is time not spent on anything else. That doesn't make infrastructure work wasted. It means it has to earn its place.

A single server. In 2026.

Kubernetes isn't the only way to run containers.

Sometimes a managed container service is enough. Sometimes a platform-as-a-service is enough. Sometimes a virtual machine with a well-understood deployment process is enough.

Sometimes a single server is all you need.

Yes. A single server. In 2026. No service mesh. No twelve microservices. No elaborate GitOps pipeline.

Just an application that works, a database that's backed up, and a deployment process that doesn't require a ritual sacrifice. Imagine that. (The database is probably Postgres, and Postgres is probably enough.)

Complexity is easy to add and hard to remove

You can always add complexity later. Migrate when the constraints are real. Adopt orchestration when managing deployments by hand actually hurts. Invest in sophisticated infrastructure when the business benefits from it.

Removing complexity after you've built the organisation around it is much harder.

Infrastructure decisions don't live in isolation. They shape hiring, team structure, developer workflows, incident response, documentation, security practices and what it costs to run the product. What starts as a technical decision becomes an organisational commitment.

Questions to ask first

Before you introduce Kubernetes, answer these honestly:

  1. What specific problem are we solving?
  2. Can our current infrastructure handle the workload?
  3. Are deployments genuinely becoming hard to manage?
  4. Do we need orchestration, or just better deployment automation?
  5. Do we have the expertise to run Kubernetes reliably?
  6. Most importantly: what evidence would convince us we need it?

If you can't answer those, you're not making an infrastructure decision. You're following a trend. And trends are a terrible reason to redesign production.

Bottom line

The goal isn't the most sophisticated infrastructure possible. It's the simplest infrastructure that reliably meets your requirements, evolved as those requirements change.

Not before. Not because another startup uses it. Not because someone on YouTube built an impressive homelab. And definitely not because Kubernetes looks good on your CV.

Use it when it solves your problems. Avoid it when it creates more than it solves.

Engineering maturity isn't about how many tools you can operate. It's about knowing which ones you don't need. Your architecture doesn't need to impress other engineers. It needs to serve your business. Sometimes the most senior decision you can make is to leave the shiny thing out.

Build the product. Get customers. Solve real problems. Let your infrastructure grow when reality demands it.

Not when your ego does.

entry.title: What a Decade of Python Taught Me About Boring Technology
entry.summary: Lessons from a decade of Python, Django and AWS: why boring technology wins, why journey tests outlive your stack, and the habits that keep systems shippable.
entry.content:
There's a version of a software career where you chase every new framework, rewrite your stack every eighteen months and spend more time on migrations than on the product. Plenty of us have done a stretch of it. The systems that last, the ones that ship features for years without drama, are almost always built on the dullest tools available.

The position: boring technology is a competitive advantage, not a compromise. Python, Django, Postgres, a load balancer and a few well-understood AWS services will take most products further than any shiny stack. The skill isn't knowing the newest tool. It's knowing when not to use it.

Boring means understood, not old

Dan McKinley's essay Choose Boring Technology put it better than anyone: a boring tool is one whose failure modes are known. You can search the error message and find the answer. You know how it behaves under load, how it breaks, and how to fix it at 2 am.

That's the real asset. Not features. Not benchmarks. Predictability.

Django is boring in exactly this way. The ORM has its sharp edges, and they're documented. The migration system has its quirks, and Stack Overflow has an answer for each one. Postgres is boring. Gunicorn is boring. SQS is boring. Every one of them has had its corner cases found by many people before you.

A new tool has failure modes too. You just don't know them yet, and you'll discover them in production.

Spend your innovation where customers notice

McKinley's other idea is the innovation token: every team gets a small number, and each new, unproven technology spends one. Spend them on what makes your product different. Not on the plumbing.

If your product is a pricing engine, innovate on pricing. Run it on Django and Postgres. If your product is a new kind of search, maybe the search engine is your token, and everything else should be as dull as possible.

The common failure is the reverse: a completely ordinary CRUD product running on a novel database, a new frontend framework, an event-sourcing library and a service mesh. Four tokens spent, none of them on anything a customer will ever see.

The habits that held up

Some lessons I'd give my younger self, in no particular order:

  • Read the standard library before installing a package. dataclasses, pathlib, itertools, functools, zoneinfo, concurrent.futures, sqlite3. Python ships a lot. Every dependency is code you didn't write and will have to upgrade.
  • Prefer a function to a class, and a module to a framework. Most abstractions people build in Python are a function with extra steps.
  • Plain SQL is a skill, not a smell. The ORM is great for 90% of queries. For the other 10%, reading EXPLAIN ANALYZE beats any amount of queryset cleverness.
  • Delete code aggressively. Dead feature flags, unused endpoints, compatibility shims for clients that no longer exist. Every line you keep is a line someone has to understand.
  • Logs and metrics before features. You can't fix what you can't see. A structured log line with a request ID has saved more incidents than any architecture change.
  • Upgrade little and often. Staying one minor version behind on Python and Django is cheap. Falling three major versions behind is a project with its own budget. I say that as someone who defended Python 2.7 long after the argument was lost.
  • Write the boring test. Not a clever property-based suite for everything. One test per business rule, named after the rule, that fails clearly.

Invest in tests that don't know how the code is written

If I could move one budget line on most teams, it would be this: spend far more on black-box tests that walk through real user journeys. Sign up. Log in. Place an order. Cancel it. Get the refund email. Drive them through the public surface, the HTTP API or the UI, and check what a user would check. Nothing else.

These tests don't import your models. They don't patch your functions. They don't know whether there's a service layer, a serializer or a stored procedure behind the endpoint. That's the point.

Everything in your stack is temporary. The framework gets a major version. The database moves. The queue gets swapped for something managed. The cloud service you picked gets deprecated. Python itself moves on, whether you're ready or not. And one day somebody will want to rewrite the whole backend.

When that day comes, everyone asks the same question: did we break the product? Unit tests tied to internals can't answer it. They die with the refactor, because they were testing the code you just deleted. A journey suite survives it. It runs against the new system exactly as it ran against the old one, and when it goes green you can say, with evidence, that the product still works.

That's why I call it an asset. It grows. Every journey you add is one more thing you can never silently break again, through any number of rewrites. Most code loses value as it ages. This suite gains it.

How I'd keep it boring:

  • Few and honest. Tens of journeys, not thousands. Cover what earns money, and what would have customers emailing you before your coffee.
  • Real dependencies. Run them in CI against a real Postgres, a real queue and real services in containers. Fake only what you don't own, like the payment provider, and fake it at the network edge.
  • Behaviour, not implementation. Assert on status codes, response bodies, emails sent, what the user can see. Never on which function got called.
  • Slow is fine. A few minutes per run is the price of honesty. Run them on every merge, not on every keystroke.
  • Cheap to keep. They don't know how the code is written, so refactors don't touch them. If a refactor breaks one, either behaviour changed or the test was peeking inside.

This is boring technology applied to testing. The journey suite is the one part of the system that doesn't care what's fashionable underneath. Rip out Django REST Framework for plain Django views (I'd encourage it) and the suite won't notice. That's exactly the predictability you want while everything else moves.

Unit tests still earn their place for tricky pure logic: date maths, pricing rules, parsers. Keep those. Just don't mistake a pile of mocks for proof that the product works.

Complexity is a loan

Every piece of complexity you add is borrowed against future time. Microservices, a second database, a message bus, a custom deploy tool. Each one might be justified. Each one charges interest: on-call load, onboarding time, upgrade work, things that can partially fail.

The question I ask now before adding anything is simple: what's the cheapest thing that could possibly work, and what evidence would make me outgrow it? Write the evidence down. "When the jobs table bloats past what autovacuum can handle." "When two teams are blocked on the same deploy." Then build the cheap thing and watch for the evidence.

Most of the time, it never shows up.

Where boring goes wrong

Boring isn't the same as stagnant. A few traps:

  • Boring isn't unmaintained. Running an end-of-life Python version isn't conservative, it's a security liability. Boring tools still need upgrades.
  • Boring isn't "what we used last time" forever. If a new tool is mature, well understood and clearly better for a real problem, like uv for Python packaging or ruff for linting, adopt it. The test is maturity and fit, not age.
  • Boring isn't refusing to learn. Learn the new things. Build side projects with them. Just don't make your production system the place where you learn them.

What actually made the difference

Looking back, the projects that went well had little to do with the stack. They had:

  1. A clear understanding of what the business actually needed this quarter.
  2. A small number of well-understood moving parts.
  3. Fast, boring deploys, many times a week.
  4. Engineers who could explain the whole system on a whiteboard.

The projects that struggled usually had an impressive architecture diagram and nobody who could explain all of it.

Bottom line

Years of Python have taught me that the most valuable engineering skill is restraint. Use the tool everyone understands. Spend novelty only where it creates value customers can feel. Keep the system small enough to fit in one head, and keep a suite of journey tests that will outlive it. It doesn't make for exciting conference talks, but it makes for software that ships, keeps shipping and lets you sleep.

entry.title: Is Your Ego Running Production?
entry.summary: Postmortems never list ego as a cause, but it's behind big-bang deploys, blame, rewrites and heroics. Public incidents, what experts say, and how to take ego out.
entry.content:
Nobody writes "ego" in the root cause field.

The postmortem says a server was missed. A command had a typo. A backup job had been failing quietly for months. Read enough of them, though, and the same shape keeps turning up behind the technical detail: someone was sure, and nothing in the system asked them to prove it.

That's what I mean by ego in production. Not arrogance as a personality trait. Certainty that outruns the evidence, and a system built to trust it.

It turns up in all sorts of places:

  • Resume-driven architecture.
  • Rewrites, because the old code "is a mess".
  • Big-bang releases that skip review because "I know this code".
  • Refusing to roll back because rolling back means admitting the change was wrong.
  • Hero on-call culture, and the blame that comes with it when the hero is the one who slipped.

The postmortems don't say ego. They say "nobody checked".

On 1 August 2012, Knight Capital deployed new code for the NYSE's Retail Liquidity Program. According to the SEC's order, a technician didn't copy the new code to one of the eight servers. The new code reused a flag that used to switch on "Power Peg", logic Knight had stopped using in 2003 but never removed. On the eighth server, that flag woke the dead code up. In about 45 minutes the router sent millions of orders into the market, and Knight lost more than $460 million.

The SEC's findings are dull, which is exactly the point. There was no second technician reviewing the deployment and no written procedure requiring one. In the SEC's words, "a written procedure requiring a simple double-check of the deployment of the RLP code could have identified that a server had been missed." It gets worse. During the incident, Knight uninstalled the new code from the seven healthy servers, and that spread the problem. Their rollback had never been designed or rehearsed. It was improvised under pressure.

On 31 January 2017, a GitLab engineer trying to rebuild database replication wiped what they thought was the secondary's data directory. It was the primary. Roughly 300 GB was gone before they stopped it. Then the backups turned out not to exist: pg_dump was running a 9.2 binary against a 9.6 database, failing every time, and the failure emails were being rejected. GitLab's postmortem names the deepest cause plainly: nobody owned testing the backups. Their conclusion is the best sentence in the whole document: "An ideal environment is one in which you can make mistakes but easily and quickly recover from them with minimal to no impact."

On 28 February 2017, an S3 engineer following an established playbook mistyped one input to a command and removed far more servers than intended in US-EAST-1. S3 was down in that region for hours. Amazon's write-up doesn't go looking for someone to blame. It fixes the tool, which "allowed too much capacity to be removed too quickly", so it now removes capacity slowly and refuses to go below a minimum.

Notice what none of these say. None of them says "the engineer was arrogant". The ego wasn't in the person at the keyboard. It was baked into a system that assumed a careful person doesn't need a check, a backup doesn't need a restore test, and a rollback doesn't need a rehearsal.

Blame is ego wearing a manager's hat

When things go wrong, the ego move is to find the person. John Allspaw, then at Etsy, called this out in Blameless PostMortems and a Just Culture, borrowing what Sidney Dekker calls the "Bad Apple Theory": get rid of the bad apples and you get rid of human error. It feels like accountability. It produces the opposite.

Allspaw's argument is that engineers have to be able to explain what they did, what they saw and what they expected, "without fear of punishment or retribution". Punish them and they go quiet. You get what he calls "Cover-Your-Ass" engineering, management stops learning how work really gets done, and the same accident comes back with a different name on it.

Richard Cook's How Complex Systems Fail goes further. Two of his points should be printed on the wall of every incident review: "Post-accident attribution to a 'root cause' is fundamentally wrong", and "Hindsight biases post-accident assessments of human performance". Failures need several things to go wrong at once. After the fact, the one human step looks obvious. It wasn't obvious at the time.

Google's SRE book puts the practical version in one line in its chapter on postmortem culture: "You can't 'fix' people, but you can fix systems and processes."

Ego in the architecture

Production incidents are the loud version. The quiet version is architecture chosen to make someone look smart.

Dan McKinley's Choose Boring Technology gives every company "about three innovation tokens". His most useful exercise is to ask how you'd solve the problem without adding anything new. Asking that, he says, catches the case where the real "problem" is that someone wants to use the technology. Resume-driven development fails that test every time. So does the Kubernetes cluster for a three-person team, and the microservices you split out before you had the teams for them. McKinley's verdict is short: "Technology for its own sake is snake oil."

Not-invented-here is the same disease aimed at libraries. Writing your own job queue, your own ORM or your own serialization layer because the existing one offends you is ego with a commit history. (Yes, DRF offends me too. The boring answer is still plain Django views, not my own framework.) And the extra database you added because Postgres felt too ordinary? Postgres was probably enough.

Then there are rewrites. Fred Brooks warned in The Mythical Man-Month about the second-system effect: confident after the first success, the designer piles every deferred idea into the next one, and that second system is "the most dangerous system a man ever designs". Joel Spolsky called rewriting from scratch "the single worst strategic mistake that any software company can make" in Things You Should Never Do, Part I. His explanation is uncomfortably personal: "It's harder to read code than to write it." The old code looks like a mess because we didn't write it. Those ugly lines are often bug fixes we don't understand yet.

Heroes, rollbacks and the 2 am fix

Every team has the engineer who saves the day at 2 am. Celebrate that often enough and you get a team that needs saving at 2 am.

The ego trap during an incident is fixing forward because rolling back feels like losing. The Google SRE book has a lovely counter-example. At a company all-hands, an engineer described a release that took down a critical service. It only lasted four minutes because he rolled it back immediately. He got two peer bonuses and a round of applause. That's the culture you want: the rollback is the heroic move.

Rollbacks only work if they're boring, though. Knight's improvised rollback made things worse. A rollback you've never practised is just another risky deploy.

Size matters too. DORA's research on software delivery, behind the book Accelerate, has found again and again that speed and stability are not tradeoffs. Their recommended lever is smaller changes: easier to reason about, easier to review, easier to recover from. A big-bang change bets everything on being right once. A small change only has to be right this time, and it's cheap when it isn't.

I'll own my bias here. I was a Python 2.7 sympathiser and a late adopter of Python 3. I know exactly how it feels to defend a position past its sell-by date. The fix isn't to never hold strong opinions. It's to know in advance what would change them.

How to tell your ego is running production

A checklist of smells:

  • "I know this code" is the reason a change skipped review or tests.
  • The release is one big change because splitting it felt like admin.
  • There's no rollback plan, or the rollback has never been run.
  • Rolling back is treated as failure rather than a normal move.
  • The new tool's main argument is that serious companies use it.
  • A rewrite is pitched as the fix for code nobody has read carefully.
  • Incident reviews end with a name rather than a change to the system.
  • The most senior voice wins design arguments that data could settle.
  • The same few people get paged, and they like it that way.
  • Nobody asks for help until the incident is an hour old.
  • "Works on my machine" ends the conversation instead of starting one.
  • Backups exist, but nobody has restored one this quarter.

What to do instead

  1. Evidence over seniority. Bring graphs, traces and load tests to design arguments. If the senior person is right, the evidence will say so.
  2. Small, reversible changes. Ship in slices behind flags. Make every deploy something you can undo in minutes.
  3. Make rollback a first-class move. Rehearse it. Automate it. Praise the person who uses it early.
  4. Two people on risky changes. A second pair of eyes on production deploys, migrations and destructive commands. That's what the SEC wanted from Knight.
  5. Guard rails in the tools. Do what Amazon did after S3: make dangerous commands slow, bounded and loud, and make it obvious which host you're on.
  6. Blameless reviews. Ask what made the action seem reasonable at the time. Fix the system, not the person.
  7. Write the decision down, with how you'd know you're wrong. Every architecture choice gets a short note covering the problem, the options and the signal that would make you reverse it.
  8. Ask "what would change my mind?" before the meeting ends. If the answer is "nothing", that's ego, not engineering.
  9. Test the restore, not the backup. Restore it on a schedule, and give someone ownership of it.

None of this is exotic. It's boring technology applied to people.

Bottom line

Production doesn't care who you are. It doesn't care how senior you are, how clever the design is or how sure you feel. It responds to small changes, real checks, rehearsed rollbacks and honest reviews.

Build systems that assume everyone, including you, will be wrong sometimes. Make being wrong cheap, quick to notice and safe to admit.

Then let the evidence run production.

Not your ego.

entry.title: Postgres Is Enough: Skip the Extra Database Until It Hurts
entry.summary: Postgres can run your job queue, full-text search, JSON documents and cache. How to do each one, with SQL and Django examples, and the signs it's time to add more.
entry.content:
Every new project seems to start with the same architecture diagram: Postgres for data, Redis for cache, RabbitMQ or SQS for jobs, Elasticsearch for search, maybe MongoDB "for the flexible stuff". Five systems to provision, secure, back up, monitor and keep consistent, for an app with three hundred users.

The position: Postgres is enough for far longer than you think. It's a queue, a search engine, a document store and a cache, all with transactions, one backup and one connection string. Add another datastore when Postgres is measurably hurting, not when a blog post says you'll need it "at scale".

The real cost of the extra box

Every additional datastore costs more than its hosting bill:

  • Consistency. Write an order to Postgres and a job to Redis. Postgres commits, Redis is unreachable. Now you have an order nobody will ever process. Or the reverse: the job runs before the transaction commits and can't find the row.
  • Operations. Another thing to patch, monitor, alert on, upgrade and restore. Another set of credentials. Another failure mode at 3 am.
  • Local development and CI. Every service is one more container in docker compose, one more thing to seed in tests.
  • Knowledge. Your team needs to understand the failure semantics of each system. Most teams deeply understand one database at best.

When the queue lives in the same database as the data, enqueuing a job is part of the same transaction. Commit the order and the job together, or neither. That one property eliminates a whole category of bugs.

A job queue with SKIP LOCKED

FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED (since Postgres 9.5) is what makes a Postgres queue practical. Workers lock the next available row and skip rows other workers already hold, so they never block on each other or grab the same job.

CREATE TABLE jobs (
    id         bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    queue      text        NOT NULL DEFAULT 'default',
    payload    jsonb       NOT NULL,
    run_at     timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    attempts   int         NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
);

CREATE INDEX jobs_ready_idx ON jobs (queue, run_at);

A worker runs this inside a transaction, does the work, then deletes the row and commits:

BEGIN;

SELECT id, payload
FROM jobs
WHERE queue = 'default' AND run_at <= now()
ORDER BY run_at
LIMIT 1
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;

-- do the work in application code, then:
DELETE FROM jobs WHERE id = $1;

COMMIT;

If the worker crashes mid-job, the transaction rolls back, the lock is released and the job becomes available again. No visibility timeouts, no lost messages. For failures you catch, bump attempts and push run_at forward for a retry with backoff.

The trade-off: the transaction stays open while the job runs, so keep jobs short. For long jobs, claim the row with a locked_until column instead, and reclaim expired ones.

You don't have to build this yourself. In Python, Procrastinate is a Postgres-backed task queue, and since Django 6.0 there's a built-in Tasks API (django.tasks) with database-backed workers available through the django-tasks-db package. Postgres also has LISTEN/NOTIFY for waking workers without polling.

Full-text search that's good enough

Before standing up Elasticsearch, try a generated tsvector column with a GIN index:

ALTER TABLE articles
    ADD COLUMN search tsvector GENERATED ALWAYS AS (
        setweight(to_tsvector('english', coalesce(title, '')), 'A') ||
        setweight(to_tsvector('english', coalesce(body, '')), 'B')
    ) STORED;

CREATE INDEX articles_search_idx ON articles USING gin (search);

SELECT id, title, ts_rank(search, query) AS rank
FROM articles,
     websearch_to_tsquery('english', 'django "service layer" -celery')
         AS query
WHERE search @@ query
ORDER BY rank DESC
LIMIT 20;

That gives you stemming ("orders" matches "order"), weighted fields, quoted phrases and exclusions through websearch_to_tsquery, which accepts the kind of syntax people type into search boxes. Add the pg_trgm extension for typo-tolerant matching on names and short strings.

Django supports this directly through django.contrib.postgres.search:

from django.contrib.postgres.search import SearchQuery, SearchRank
from django.db.models import F

query = SearchQuery("django service layer",
                    search_type="websearch", config="english")
results = (
    Article.objects.filter(search=query)
    .annotate(rank=SearchRank(F("search"), query))
    .order_by("-rank")[:20]
)

It won't match a dedicated search engine on relevance tuning, faceting at huge scale or multi-language analysis. For a product catalogue, a help centre or an admin search box, it's usually plenty.

JSON when the schema really is flexible

jsonb stores JSON in a binary, indexable form. Need to store webhook payloads, per-tenant settings or third-party API responses? You don't need a document database.

CREATE INDEX events_payload_idx ON events USING gin (payload jsonb_path_ops);

SELECT id FROM events WHERE payload @> '{"type": "invoice.paid"}';

In Django, models.JSONField maps to jsonb on Postgres, and lookups like filter(payload__type="invoice.paid") work out of the box.

One warning: jsonb is a pressure valve, not a design. If you're querying the same keys in every request, they're columns. Promote them.

A cache that's one table

For many apps the "cache" is a handful of expensive computed values. Postgres can hold those in an UNLOGGED table, which skips the write-ahead log, so writes are cheaper. The catch is that it's truncated after a crash, which is exactly the durability a cache needs.

CREATE UNLOGGED TABLE cache (
    key        text PRIMARY KEY,
    value      jsonb NOT NULL,
    expires_at timestamptz NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO cache (key, value, expires_at)
VALUES ('dashboard:42', '{"orders": 118}', now() + interval '5 minutes')
ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE
    SET value = EXCLUDED.value, expires_at = EXCLUDED.expires_at;

Django also ships a database cache backend, django.core.cache.backends.db.DatabaseCache, set up with manage.py createcachetable. Before you add a cache at all, check whether the real fix is an index, a select_related() or a materialized view.

When it actually hurts

I'm not saying never. I'm saying wait for evidence. Signs that it's time:

  • Queue throughput. Sustained high job volume where the jobs table churns faster than autovacuum keeps up, and the bloat shows in your metrics. That's when SQS or a dedicated broker earns its keep.
  • Cache hit volume. You need very high read rates on hot keys with sub-millisecond latency, and the cache traffic is competing with your real queries for connections and CPU. That's what Redis or Valkey is for.
  • Search quality. Users need faceting, synonyms, typo tolerance across large corpora or relevance tuning you can't get from ts_rank. Bring in OpenSearch, Meilisearch or similar.
  • Analytics. Large aggregations over hundreds of millions of rows slow down the primary. Move them to a replica first, then to a columnar store if needed.
  • Fan-out and streaming. Many consumers replaying an event log is Kafka's job, not a jobs table.

Every one of those is a measurement, not a feeling. Watch query latency, connection count, replication lag, table bloat and CPU. When a specific workload is the cause, extract that workload, and only that one.

Bottom line

Postgres has decades of engineering behind it, transactions across everything you put in it, and one backup story. Start with one database. Use it properly. Add the second system when a graph tells you to, not when a diagram does. Most products never get there, and the ones that do will know exactly which piece to move out.

entry.title: Lambda Is Not Cheap: When Serverless Costs More Than a Boring EC2 Box
entry.summary: AWS Lambda bills wall-clock time per request, so steady traffic can cost more than an EC2 box. The formula, a worked example, cold starts and when Lambda wins.
entry.content:
"Serverless is cheaper" is one of those lines that gets repeated until nobody checks it. For a cron job that runs twice a day, it's true. For a Django API with steady traffic, it's often false, sometimes by a wide margin, and the bill arrives after the architecture is already committed.

The position: Lambda is priced per unit of work, EC2 is priced per unit of time. Below a certain steady load, per-work wins. Above it, the boring box wins, and the crossover comes sooner than people expect. You can work out where yours is with a calculator and ten minutes. Most teams never do.

How Lambda actually bills

The pricing model is simple, which is exactly why it's easy to underestimate:

  • A request charge per invocation.
  • A duration charge in GB-seconds: allocated memory multiplied by the time your function runs, billed per millisecond.
  • A free tier of 1 million requests and 400,000 GB-seconds per month.
  • Since 1 August 2025, the INIT phase is billed for on-demand ZIP functions on managed runtimes too. Cold start time is now part of your bill, not just your latency.
  • Extras around it: API Gateway or a function URL in front, CloudWatch Logs for every invocation, NAT gateway charges if your function sits in a VPC and calls the internet, and provisioned concurrency if you buy your way out of cold starts.

As of February 2026, the AWS pricing page lists x86 on-demand duration at $0.0000166667 per GB-second and requests at $0.20 per million, in its worked example. Prices vary by region and Arm (Graviton) is cheaper per GB-second, so check your own region before you plug in numbers.

The part everybody misses: you pay for waiting

A typical Django endpoint doesn't compute much. It receives a request, runs a few queries, maybe calls another service, serialises JSON. Most of its wall-clock time is spent waiting on I/O.

On an EC2 box, that waiting is nearly free. While one request waits on Postgres, the same process, through threads, async or more workers, serves others. One instance overlaps hundreds of waiting requests.

On default Lambda, each execution environment handles one request at a time, and you're billed for its full duration, waiting included. A 200 ms request that spends 180 ms waiting on the database costs you 200 ms of allocated memory. Lambda bills you for the time your code is idle.

That's the structural reason I/O-heavy, steady-traffic APIs tend to be expensive on Lambda. It's not a pricing trick. It's the model.

The formula

Per month, ignoring the free tier:

lambda_cost = R * (P_req + d * m * P_gbs)

R      = requests per month
P_req  = price per request           (e.g. 0.20 / 1,000,000)
d      = average billed duration, s  (include INIT for cold starts)
m      = allocated memory, GB
P_gbs  = price per GB-second         (e.g. 0.0000166667)

The cost per request is the bracket. Break-even against a fixed monthly server cost E is simply:

break_even_requests = E / (P_req + d * m * P_gbs)

As code, so you can play with it:

SECONDS_PER_MONTH = 30 * 24 * 3600


def lambda_monthly(rps: float, duration_s: float, memory_gb: float,
                   p_req: float = 0.20 / 1_000_000,
                   p_gbs: float = 0.0000166667) -> float:
    requests = rps * SECONDS_PER_MONTH
    return requests * (p_req + duration_s * memory_gb * p_gbs)


def break_even_rps(server_monthly: float, duration_s: float, memory_gb: float,
                   p_req: float = 0.20 / 1_000_000,
                   p_gbs: float = 0.0000166667) -> float:
    per_request = p_req + duration_s * memory_gb * p_gbs
    return server_monthly / per_request / SECONDS_PER_MONTH


print(round(lambda_monthly(50, 0.2, 1.0), 2))      # 457.92
print(round(break_even_rps(150, 0.2, 1.0), 1))     # 16.4

A worked example (illustrative numbers)

These are made-up but realistic inputs, not a benchmark. Change them to yours.

  • An API averaging 50 requests per second, all month.
  • 200 ms average duration, 1 GB of memory.
  • That's about 129.6 million requests a month.

Lambda, before the free tier, API Gateway, logs or NAT:

  • Requests: 129.6M x $0.20 per million = about $26
  • Duration: 129.6M x 0.2 s x 1 GB = 25.9M GB-s, x $0.0000166667 = about $432
  • Total: about $458 a month, and that's before the extras.

Now suppose your alternative, a pair of modest instances behind a load balancer for redundancy, costs $150 a month (an illustrative figure, not a quote; price your own instance types). The break-even is about 16 requests per second of average load. Above that, every extra request widens the gap in the box's favour, because the box costs the same whether it's 20% or 70% busy.

Notice what moves the answer most: duration and memory. Halve your average duration and Lambda's duration bill halves. Teams that cut Lambda bills mostly do it by making functions faster or smaller, which is a fine outcome. But it's the same work that makes a box handle more load.

Cold starts are a cost, not just a delay

Django is not a small import. Load settings, the ORM, apps, DRF, a few SDKs, and the init phase can take a noticeable fraction of a second. Since INIT is billed, every cold start is paid time. The options all cost something:

  • Provisioned concurrency keeps environments warm, and you pay for it by the hour whether requests arrive or not. Which is, functionally, a server.
  • SnapStart for Python restores from a snapshot to cut init time, with its own charges and caveats around anything that must be unique per environment, like random seeds and connections.
  • Slimming the package and lazy imports help, and they're worth doing anyway.

And then there's the database. Hundreds of concurrent Lambda environments each opening a Postgres connection will exhaust max_connections quickly. The fix is RDS Proxy or another pooler, which is another line on the bill and another moving part.

Where Lambda genuinely wins

I'm not anti-Lambda. I'm anti-assuming. It's excellent when:

  • Traffic is spiky or near zero most of the time. Internal tools, webhooks, a back-office API used during business hours. Scale to zero is real money.
  • It's event glue. S3 upload triggers, SQS consumers, EventBridge rules, small transforms between AWS services. This is what Lambda was built for and it's hard to beat.
  • Scheduled jobs. A nightly report doesn't justify an always-on box.
  • Parallel bursts. Fan out thousands of independent tasks for five minutes, then nothing.
  • You have no one to run servers. Patching, scaling and replacing instances is real work. If nobody on the team will do it, that labour has a cost too, and it can outweigh the bill difference. Just count it honestly rather than assuming it's huge.

Note the shape: Lambda wins when utilisation would be low on a server. The less steady the traffic, the better it looks.

The boring middle ground

It isn't Lambda or a hand-built pet server. A Django app in a container on ECS with Fargate, or an EC2 Auto Scaling group behind a load balancer, gives you managed deploys, health checks and scaling while keeping the concurrency model where one process serves many waiting requests. Add a Compute Savings Plan or reserved capacity for the baseline and your steady load gets cheaper still. AWS itself launched Lambda Managed Instances in late 2025: functions run on EC2 instances, several requests share an execution environment, and you pay EC2 instance prices plus a management fee and the usual request charge, instead of per-request duration. When the vendor ships that hybrid for steady workloads, the trade-off is real.

How to decide

  1. Pull a month of real traffic. Get average requests per second and the peak-to-average ratio.
  2. Measure average billed duration and memory from your Lambda REPORT log lines, or estimate from your current app's response times.
  3. Run the formula. Add API Gateway, logs, NAT and any provisioned concurrency.
  4. Price the boring alternative honestly, including redundancy and a bit of headroom.
  5. If Lambda is cheaper, or close and the ops savings matter, use it. If it's several times more, stop calling it the cheap option.

Bottom line

Lambda bills you for every millisecond your code waits on a database. That's perfect for bursty, event-driven and low-traffic work, and expensive for steady APIs. Do the arithmetic before the architecture diagram. The boring EC2 box doesn't have a conference talk, but it often has the smaller invoice.

entry.title: Store Every Datetime as Naive Asia:Shanghai
entry.summary: Why I store every datetime as naive Asia/Shanghai (UTC+8, no DST) instead of UTC, how Chinese platforms already work this way, and the case for UTZ offsets.
entry.content:
After more than a decade of fighting timezone bugs across distributed systems, I made a deliberate, non-reversible decision in late 2022:

Every TIMESTAMP and DATETIME column in my production databases is stored naive (timezone-unaware) and interpreted as Asia/Shanghai (UTC+8, no DST).

No timestamptz. No UTC. No per-user offset metadata. Just clean, fixed-offset naive values in what is effectively Beijing-local time.

At first glance this looks heretical. The orthodox answer is still "always store in UTC". Yet after implementing this pattern at scale, the results are hard to argue with: drastically fewer bugs, simpler debugging, cleaner cron/scheduling logic, and - most importantly - alignment with where the majority of my users, traffic, and revenue actually live.

More strikingly: this is not an eccentric personal choice. It is already the reality inside the world's largest digital ecosystem.

Chinese platforms already operate on what we might call utz+0

WeChat, Alipay, Douyin / TikTok (domestic), Pinduoduo - virtually every consumer-facing Chinese super-app stores and computes time as naive Asia/Shanghai.

  • Transaction logs, user activity events, payment timestamps -> all naive UTC+8
  • Delivery ETAs, driver assignment windows, flash-sale timers -> calculated and stored in Beijing time
  • Billing cycles, daily analytics batches, fraud-detection windows -> anchored to Shanghai clock
  • Even many backend cron jobs and monitoring dashboards assume UTC+8 as the implicit reference

This isn't accidental. When you serve 1.4 billion people whose daily life (work, school, meals, sleep) already orbits Beijing time, imposing UTC adds pointless conversion overhead at every layer.

The Chinese mantra goes something like this, instead of adapting to the world, the world starts adapting to you.

Add Singapore, Malaysia, Philippines, Brunei, Indonesia, Mongolia, and Perth - all already on UTC+8 - and you have a coherent bloc of ~2 billion people already living and transacting on what I now informally call UTZ (Universal Temporal Zone = Asia/Shanghai = UTC+8, no DST).

Reframing the world in UTZ offsets

Once you recenter the map on Beijing instead of Greenwich, the numbers become elegantly simple for the most populous part of the planet:

Region UTC UTZ Population
Beijing, Singapore, Manila, KL, Perth, Indonesia UTC+8 UTZ+0 ~2.0B+
Tokyo, Seoul, Pyongyang UTC+9 UTZ+1 ~200M
Bangkok, Hanoi, Vientiane, Phnom Penh UTC+7 UTZ-1 ~220M
Delhi UTC+5:30 UTZ-2.5 ~1.4B
Sydney / Melbourne UTC+10 UTZ+2 ~26M
London UTC+1 UTZ-7 -
New York UTC-4 UTZ-12 -

For ~50% of humanity, time suddenly feels centered rather than perpetually "ahead" or "behind".

How the shift gains momentum - a realistic, economics-driven roadmap

No IETF RFC or UN resolution will declare UTZ. Change will come through economic gravity, platform lock-in, infrastructure dependencies, and soft (but very real) incentives - forces already in motion.

Here are some of my predictions with respect to timezone adaptation. To accelerate this shift, Beijing must proactively wield soft power—issuing formal invitations backed by economic incentives and diplomatic charm—or, if resistance persists, apply subtle coercion through platform dominance and infrastructure dependencies.

Phase 1 - Core Already Secured
China + Mongolia + Singapore + Malaysia + Philippines + Brunei + Indonesia + Perth = ~2B people effectively on UTZ+0 today. No action required. The foundation exists.

Phase 2 - High-Leverage Neighbors (Very Plausible Next 5-10 Years)
Beijing should lead with official invitations to these neighbors, framing alignment as a mutual win for prosperity and efficiency. If soft appeals fall short, leverage economic ties for gentle coercion.

  • Tokyo / Seoul / Pyongyang (UTC+9 -> UTZ+0)
    Leverage: semiconductor supply chains, cloud & CDN dependencies, content distribution deals (anime, K-pop, games via Chinese platforms), massive Chinese tourism & student flows.
    Framing: "Your digital economy already runs on infrastructure timed to Beijing. Why keep forcing one-hour conversions everywhere?"
  • Bangkok / Hanoi / Vientiane / Phnom Penh (UTC+7 -> UTZ+0)
    Leverage: Belt & Road rail/highway/port projects, cross-border e-commerce (Shopee, Lazada, Temu), payment rails (Alipay / WeChat Pay integration), massive SME seller base on Chinese platforms.
    Framing: "Your delivery riders, street vendors, and exporters already live in our apps. One shared clock = faster growth, fewer disputes."

Achieving these shifts alone brings ~2.3-2.5 billion people under a unified temporal framework - roughly one third of humanity, concentrated in the world's growth center.

Phase 3 - Broader Platform & Financial Pull

  • Stock exchanges & market hours begin syncing to a common UTZ window (e.g., 09:30 UTZ+0 open for Shanghai / Shenzhen / HK -> Tokyo / Seoul follow, then Jakarta / Bangkok adjust). Algo-trading desks and index funds hate timezone math; they will quietly reward alignment.
  • Global developers building mini-programs, TikTok Shop, or Douyin international increasingly default to naive Asia/Shanghai timestamps.

Once critical economic flows (trade settlements, ad impressions, delivery SLAs) assume UTZ, civil-time adjustments become the path of least resistance.

Why I commit to naive Asia/Shanghai storage today

  • My largest user cohorts and fastest-growing revenue streams are already in UTZ-aligned regions.
  • My primary regions (Singapore / Shanghai VPCs) run natively in UTC+8.
  • Business events (peak usage, flash campaigns, financial cutoffs) are defined by "Beijing morning" - not Greenwich midnight.
  • Naive storage + consistent interpretation eliminates classes of bugs that have haunted every multi-region system I've ever inherited.

I'm not doing this out of sentiment. I'm doing it because the data, the traffic maps, and the platform momentum all point the same way.

UTC was the right default when the internet was young and Western-centric. But infrastructure follows users, users follow economic centers, and economic mass has decisively shifted.

Final thought

Time is not purely technical - it is infrastructural, and infrastructure follows power.

UTZ isn't a proposal. It's already partially deployed at planetary scale.

The only remaining question is how long the rest of the industry takes to notice Who knows... one day the Forbidden Kingdom might even become the prime meridian with 0° longitude.

That goes without saying:

One Belt, One Road, One TZ.

entry.title: Type Hints Pay Off Only If You Run a Type Checker in CI
entry.summary: Python type hints are just comments until mypy or pyright runs in CI. A pragmatic guide to gradual adoption, config that works and rules worth keeping.
entry.content:
Python type hints have a dirty secret: the interpreter ignores them. def total(x: int) -> int will happily accept a string and return a list. Nothing checks it at runtime unless you add a library that does. Annotations are metadata. Nothing more.

So here's the position: type hints without a type checker in CI are decorative comments that can lie. Worse than no hints, because they look authoritative. If you're going to write them, make a machine verify them on every pull request. If you're not going to do that, at least be honest that they're documentation.

Hints that lie

This is the failure mode in a codebase where hints are written but never checked:

def find_user(email: str) -> User:
    return User.objects.filter(email=email).first()

That annotation is false. .first() returns None when nothing matches. Every caller trusts the signature, skips the None check, and the bug surfaces as AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'name' in production, three calls away from the cause.

A type checker with the Django plugin flags this immediately: the function returns User | None, not User. The fix is one honest annotation:

def find_user(email: str) -> User | None:
    return User.objects.filter(email=email).first()

Now every caller is forced to handle the missing case, and the checker tells you which ones don't. That's the entire value proposition of typing: move a class of runtime errors to review time. It only works if something actually runs.

Pick a checker and stop debating

The mainstream options:

  • mypy - the original, maintained under the Python organisation, with a mature plugin system. If you use Django, the django-stubs plugin makes querysets and model fields understood. This is the default choice for Django projects.
  • pyright - Microsoft's checker, written in TypeScript and fast. It powers the Pylance extension in VS Code, so many developers already see its errors in their editor. Its inference is aggressive and its strict mode is strict.
  • Newer Rust-based checkers such as Astral's ty and Meta's Pyrefly are worth watching. Check their status before betting a large codebase on them.

My advice: Django-heavy codebase, start with mypy and django-stubs. Library or non-Django service, pyright is a great default. Either is far better than neither, and arguing about it for a sprint is worse than picking one today.

Gradual adoption that doesn't stall

The common mistake is turning on --strict across a 200,000-line codebase, seeing thousands of errors and giving up. Python typing is designed to be gradual. Use that.

Start permissive globally and strict where it matters:

# pyproject.toml
[tool.mypy]
python_version = "3.12"
plugins = ["mypy_django_plugin.main"]
warn_unused_ignores = true
warn_redundant_casts = true
no_implicit_optional = true
check_untyped_defs = true

[tool.django-stubs]
django_settings_module = "config.settings"

# New and critical code: no untyped functions allowed.
[[tool.mypy.overrides]]
module = ["billing.*", "orders.services", "orders.selectors"]
disallow_untyped_defs = true
disallow_any_generics = true
warn_return_any = true

# Third-party packages without stubs: don't let them block CI.
[[tool.mypy.overrides]]
module = ["legacy_vendor_sdk.*"]
ignore_missing_imports = true

Then ratchet:

  1. Week one: run the checker in CI on the whole repo with the permissive defaults. Fix or # type: ignore[code] the existing errors. The goal is a green baseline, not perfection.
  2. Every new module goes into the strict override list. New code is typed from birth.
  3. Every time you touch an old module for real work, add it to the strict list and fix what falls out. Leave the place better than you found it.
  4. Track the ignore count. grep -rc "type: ignore" in CI is crude and it works. The number should only go down.

warn_unused_ignores matters more than it looks. When you fix the underlying problem, the stale ignore becomes an error, so suppressions can't rot silently.

Wire it into CI, not just the editor

Editor squiggles are advisory. A red CI check is a rule. A minimal GitHub Actions job:

name: typecheck
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  mypy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v6
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      - run: pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
      - run: mypy .

Pin your checker version in requirements-dev.txt. Checkers get smarter with each release, which means an unpinned upgrade can turn a green build red on a Monday morning with no code change. Upgrade on purpose, in its own pull request.

Make the check required on the main branch. If it can be skipped, it will be.

Rules worth keeping

Typing everything perfectly isn't the goal. Typing the parts where bugs are expensive is.

  • Type the boundaries first. Public functions, service layers, anything another module calls. Internals of a twenty-line helper can wait.
  • Ban Any from spreading. Any is contagious: whatever touches it becomes unchecked. Use it at the edge, such as parsing raw JSON, then convert to a real type immediately.
  • Model data, don't pass dicts. A dict[str, Any] travelling through five functions is a bug farm. Use a dataclass for internal data and a TypedDict when the shape really is a dict, like a JSON payload.
  • Use Protocol for dependencies. It's structural typing: a fake in tests satisfies it without inheriting anything.
from decimal import Decimal
from typing import Protocol


class PaymentGateway(Protocol):
    def charge(
        self, *, customer_id: str, amount: Decimal, reference: str
    ) -> str: ...


def settle(gateway: PaymentGateway, customer_id: str, amount: Decimal) -> str:
    return gateway.charge(
        customer_id=customer_id, amount=amount, reference="manual"
    )
  • Every ignore carries an error code. # type: ignore[attr-defined], never a bare # type: ignore. Bare ignores hide every future error on that line too.
  • Use reveal_type() when confused. Drop it in, run the checker, read what it thinks. It beats guessing.
  • Don't fight the checker with cast(). Each cast is you overruling the machine. Sometimes you're right. Usually the type is wrong upstream.

What typing won't do

Be clear-eyed about it. A type checker won't validate data coming over the wire. Your request body is still untrusted bytes, and for that you want runtime validation: a serializer, Pydantic or a plain schema check. Typing also won't catch logic bugs where the types line up and the maths is wrong. That's what tests are for.

Types and tests aren't competitors. Types eliminate a whole category of tests you'd otherwise write: "what if this is None", "what if someone passes a string". Tests cover behaviour. Together they're cheaper than either alone.

The cost argument

The usual objection is speed: "annotations slow us down." For a throwaway script, sure, skip them. For code that lives longer than a quarter and is touched by more than one person, the trade usually goes the other way. Refactoring is where it shows. Rename a field, change a return type, split a function, and the checker gives you the list of every call site that needs to change. Without it, that list is "grep and hope".

Bottom line

A type hint is a promise. A type checker in CI is what makes the promise binding. Pick mypy or pyright, start permissive, make new code strict, ratchet old code as you touch it, and make the check required. If you're not going to run a checker, stop writing hints that might be wrong. Unverified types aren't documentation, they're rumours.

entry.title: DST Is a Bug, Not a Feature
entry.summary: Daylight saving time causes twice-yearly software bugs. A look at countries that dropped DST, from Russia and China to Iceland and Turkey, and what devs can learn.
entry.content:
Daylight Saving Time isn't "saving" anything. It's a 100-year-old hack that introduces twice-yearly bugs into every system that touches schedules, logs, billing, notifications, cron jobs, and human sanity.

We advance clocks in spring → people lose an hour of sleep → heart attacks spike slightly, accidents go up, life satisfaction dips. Fall back → everyone celebrates the "extra hour" until they realize it's just redistributing misery. Energy savings? Negligible or negative in modern AC-heavy worlds. Developer pain? Infinite.

Yet somehow, most of Europe and North America still run this circus. Meanwhile, a growing list of countries said "nah" and haven't looked back. Let's meet the defectors who fixed their timezone code and moved on with fixed offsets forever.

1. Russia (abolished 2014, after a brief "permanent DST" experiment gone wrong)

Tried permanent summer time 2011–2014 → dark winter mornings, kids going to school in pitch black, massive complaints. Switched back to permanent standard time (winter time) in 2014. Result? No more biannual chaos, simpler scheduling across 11 time zones (now 11 again after earlier cuts), no regrets reported. Russians just shrugged and kept living. If a country spanning ~11 time zones can ditch the switch without imploding, your app can too.

2. China (tried 1986–1991, abolished permanently)

Short experiment for "energy conservation." Saved a bit of kWh in theory, but caused massive confusion-people forgot to change clocks, meetings double-booked, factories messed up. Government killed it in 1992 citing "inconvenience." China never looked back. One timezone (UTC+8, no DST ever), 1.4B+ people, zero clock-change bugs in WeChat/Alipay/Douyin. Coincidence? I think not. They basically run on naive Asia/Shanghai everywhere and it scales beautifully.

3. Iceland (abolished effectively since 1968, permanent UTC+0)

Way up north with insane summer daylight anyway (midnight sun vibes). Tried DST briefly, ditched it because extending already-long days made zero sense. No clock changes since the late 60s. Icelanders just live with consistent time. Productivity didn't collapse. Northern lights still appear. Win.

4. Turkey (switched to permanent DST in 2016 → effectively no more changes)

They didn't "abolish" the switch so much as lock it on summer time forever (UTC+3 year-round). No fall-back. No spring-forward. Just fixed. Energy arguments aside, no biannual disruptions. Business goes on.

5. Recent dropouts (last 10–15 years): Armenia, Azerbaijan, Belarus, Georgia, Iran, Jordan, Namibia, Samoa, Syria, Uruguay

These are the fresh ones. Jordan/Syria went permanent summer time recently (2022). Namibia, Uruguay ditched after trials showed meh energy gains and lots of hassle. Iran bounced for religious/political reasons but stayed off. Pattern? Once you stop the twice-yearly jolt, nobody riots to bring it back. The switch is the bug; fixed offset is the stable release.

For Australia the story is entirely different, Australia - the chaotic half-defector that accidentally proved the point. Australia is the ultimate “we tried DST and mostly hated it” exhibit.

Three mainland states (Queensland, Western Australia, Northern Territory) never observe DST and have been on permanent standard time forever. Queensland in particular has been loud about it since 1992 - they tried it, voters hated the late sunsets messing with kids’ bedtimes and farmers’ routines, and they killed it permanently. No regrets.

The other states (NSW, Victoria, SA, Tasmania, ACT) still do the biannual dance… but even there, every few years someone floats “permanent summer time” or “permanent standard” and the public usually says “just pick one and leave it alone.” Result? A country with wildly inconsistent rules across borders, yet the non-DST states report zero chaos compared to the ones that still flip. Queensland businesses schedule with Brisbane time year-round, no bugs, no double-booked Zoom calls, no “did the meeting move because of DST?” drama. Meanwhile Sydney/Melbourne teams still deal with the March/October ritual.

Australia basically runs a live A/B test: half the country on fixed offset, half still running legacy code. Guess which half has fewer timezone-support tickets? Fixed wins. Bonus honorable mentions:

Arizona (most of it, since 1968) - Hot desert + DST = more AC runtime in evenings = higher bills. Opted out permanently. Navajo Nation still does DST for border reasons, but the state as a whole? Nope.

Most equatorial/tropical countries - Never bothered in the first place. Daylight barely varies year-round. Why add bugs when nature already gave you a stable API?

What These Countries Teach Us Devs

  • Biannual changes are non-deterministic garbage injected into otherwise predictable systems.
  • Permanent fixed offset = fewer edge cases (no "did this event happen before/after the switch?"), simpler queries, no timezone DB updates breaking prod every March/October.
  • "But energy savings!" - Modern studies show it's a wash or net negative. Countries that quit report no measurable regret spike.
  • Humans adapt fast to fixed local wall-clock time. Meetings at 9 AM stay 9 AM forever. Cron jobs don't ghost or double-fire.

DST isn't a feature. It's technical debt the world is slowly paying off.

entry.title: Why Microservices Are a Luxury Tax on Startups
entry.summary: Why microservices are a luxury tax on startups: the deployment, network, data-consistency and cloud-cost overhead they add, and why modular monoliths keep winning.
entry.content:
It's 2025 and the discourse is still stuck in 2015: "Microservices = scale. Monoliths = legacy." Meanwhile, real startups are bleeding runway, burning investor cash, and dying on pagers because they chased distributed-system porn before they even had product-market fit.

The truth nobody wants to tweet: Microservices are mostly a luxury tax-a massive up-front cost in complexity, ops, debugging, and velocity that 90%+ of startups can't afford until way later (if ever). Monoliths, especially well-modularized ones, keep winning at actual scale for most companies that aren't Netflix or Amazon.

The tax breakdown: What you're actually paying for

You don't get "scale" for free with microservices. You pay in blood:

  • Deployment & ops hell - Separate repos/services = separate CI/CD pipelines, separate deploys, separate monitoring, separate rollbacks. One tiny auth service down? Good luck tracing why your whole app is 500-ing. A monolith? git push - build - deploy once. Velocity stays high when your team is 5–15 people.

  • Network tax everywhere - In-process function calls become 10–100 ms RPCs (or worse with retries/backoffs). Latency compounds. Debugging distributed traces feels like archaeology. Monolith? Method call is microseconds, stack traces are instant.

  • Data consistency roulette - Each service wants its own DB (cool story). Now you have eventual consistency, sagas, 2PC nightmares, or duplicated data. Monolith shares one DB transaction-boom, ACID for free where it matters.

  • Coordination overhead - API contracts, versioning, backward compat, service discovery, circuit breakers, rate limiting per service. All that boilerplate before you ship your first feature. Monolith? Just refactor a module and commit.

  • Cost tax - More containers/pods = more cloud bill (even tiny ones eat RAM/CPU overhead). Orchestration (K8s) needs dedicated SRE time. Startups pay engineers to fight infra instead of building product.

Real numbers from trenches (anecdotal but repeated across Reddit/HN/startup war stories): teams that go micro early often see 2–5× slower iteration speed until they hit 50+ engineers. By then, many are already dead or pivoted.

Who actually wins with monoliths at "scale"?

Not just tiny MVPs-these are production beasts handling real traffic:

  • Stack Overflow - Still a modular monolith (ASP.NET). Millions of users, high traffic, legendary performance. They vertical-scale + optimize queries/caching and laugh at microservice FOMO.

  • Shopify - Ruby monolith for core (they extract when needed, but the heart stays monolithic). Handles Black Friday insanity without rewriting everything.

  • Basecamp - Rails monolith forever. Deliberately simple, scales to enterprise customers without distributed drama.

  • Many "successful" unicorns pre-unicorn - Almost all start monolith (Shopify, Basecamp, early Stripe vibes, plenty of SaaS quietly). They extract services surgically only when pain is proven (e.g., one hot path kills perf - pull it out).

Even big players backtrack: Amazon Prime Video famously ditched microservices/serverless for a monolith-ish approach on some workloads because the overhead was killing cost/efficiency at real scale.

The honest startup playbook

  1. Start monolithic (modular from day 1-clean boundaries, dependency injection, bounded contexts). Ship fast, validate idea, get paying users.

  2. Scale vertically first - Bigger instances, read replicas, caching (Redis), query optimization, CDNs. Handles 100k–1M+ users for most SaaS/apps without drama.

  3. Extract only when you have concrete pain -

    • Team coordination hell? (multiple teams blocked) - extract team-owned services.
    • One component eats all resources? - pull it out (e.g., reporting, image processing).
    • Need independent deploys/tech stacks? - micro now makes sense.

  4. Prefer modular monolith - Hexagonal/ports-and-adapters, domain-driven design modules. Refactor feels like surgery, not heart transplant. When extraction time comes, boundaries already exist.

  5. Kill the FOMO - "But Netflix/Amazon/Uber!" - They had 1000+ engineers and billions in revenue before microservices became mandatory. You're not them (yet). Premature microservices is how you turn a $2M seed into $1M infra bill and zero product.

Bottom line in 2025: Monoliths aren't dead-they're the cheat code for velocity and survival. Microservices are a luxury tax you pay when you have luxury problems (big teams, uneven scaling, org-scale coordination). Most startups never reach that luxury. They die trying to afford it.

The ones that win? They ship relentlessly in a monolith until the monolith screams for mercy-then (and only then) they pay the tax.

entry.title: Stop Putting Business Logic in Django Views and Serializers
entry.summary: Why Django business logic belongs in plain service functions, not views or DRF serializers, with a before/after order example and tests that need no HTTP.
entry.content:
Open any Django codebase that's older than eighteen months and find the most important thing the business does. Placing an order. Approving a loan. Issuing a refund. Now find where that logic lives. Nine times out of ten it's smeared across a view, a serializer's create(), two model save() overrides and a post_save signal somebody added on a Friday.

Here's the position: views and serializers are adapters, not homes. A view translates HTTP into a function call. A serializer translates JSON into Python values. Neither should know what an order is. Put the rules in plain Python functions that take plain arguments, and your app gets easier to test, easier to read and much easier to change.

How it goes wrong

Nobody decides to put business logic in a serializer. It happens because Django and DRF make the wrong place the convenient place:

  • ModelSerializer.create() is right there. It already has validated data and a model. Adding "and also charge the card" is one line.
  • Views have the request. The user, the headers, the session. So the logic that needs the user ends up next to the request.
  • Signals look clean. Until nobody can tell you what happens when an Order is saved, because the answer is spread over four apps.
  • Fat models sound like good advice. And they are, for logic about one row. They fall apart when a use case touches five models and an external API.

The result is logic you can only reach through HTTP. Want to place an order from a management command, a Celery task or a data migration? You either fake a request or copy the code. Both are bad.

Before: the serializer that does everything

This is a composite of code I've seen many times. It works. It's also a trap.

class OrderSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):
    items = OrderItemSerializer(many=True)

    class Meta:
        model = Order
        fields = ["id", "items", "total"]
        read_only_fields = ["total"]

    def create(self, validated_data):
        items = validated_data.pop("items")
        user = self.context["request"].user
        order = Order.objects.create(customer=user, total=0)
        total = Decimal("0")
        for item in items:
            product = item["product"]
            if product.stock < item["quantity"]:
                raise serializers.ValidationError("Out of stock")
            product.stock -= item["quantity"]
            product.save()
            OrderItem.objects.create(order=order, product=product,
                                     quantity=item["quantity"],
                                     price=product.price)
            total += product.price * item["quantity"]
        order.total = total
        order.save()
        stripe.PaymentIntent.create(amount=int(total * 100), currency="aud",
                                    customer=user.stripe_id)
        send_mail("Order received", f"Order {order.id}", None, [user.email])
        return order

Count the problems:

  1. No transaction. If the payment call fails, you've already decremented stock and created a half-built order.
  2. A race on stock. Two requests read stock = 1, both pass the check, both save 0. You've sold the same item twice.
  3. The email goes out before anything is committed. The customer gets "Order received" for an order that may roll back.
  4. The rules are tied to self.context["request"]. You can't call this without an HTTP request, or a fake one.
  5. A ValidationError for a business rule. "Out of stock" isn't malformed input. It's a domain outcome, and it deserves its own type.
  6. Testing it means testing everything. To check the stock rule you need a client, auth, JSON and a mocked Stripe.

After: a service function

Make a services.py (or orders/services/place_order.py when it grows) with a plain function. Keyword-only arguments, explicit dependencies, a clear return type.

# orders/services.py
from dataclasses import dataclass
from decimal import Decimal

from django.db import transaction
from django.db.models import F

from orders.models import Order, OrderItem, Product
from orders.notifications import send_order_received


class OutOfStock(Exception):
    def __init__(self, product_id: int) -> None:
        super().__init__(f"Product {product_id} is out of stock")
        self.product_id = product_id


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class LineRequest:
    product_id: int
    quantity: int


def place_order(*, customer, lines: list[LineRequest], payments) -> Order:
    with transaction.atomic():
        ids = sorted({line.product_id for line in lines})
        locked = (Product.objects.select_for_update()
                  .filter(pk__in=ids).order_by("pk"))
        products = {product.pk: product for product in locked}

        order = Order.objects.create(customer=customer, total=Decimal("0"))
        total = Decimal("0")
        for line in lines:
            product = products[line.product_id]
            if product.stock < line.quantity:
                raise OutOfStock(product.pk)
            Product.objects.filter(pk=product.pk).update(
                stock=F("stock") - line.quantity)
            OrderItem.objects.create(order=order, product=product,
                                     quantity=line.quantity,
                                     price=product.price)
            total += product.price * line.quantity

        order.total = total
        order.save(update_fields=["total"])
        payments.charge(customer=customer, amount=total,
                        reference=str(order.pk))
        transaction.on_commit(lambda: send_order_received(order.pk))
    return order

What changed:

  • transaction.atomic() wraps the whole use case. Any exception, including a payment failure, rolls back the stock and the order.
  • select_for_update() locks the product rows, in a stable order, so two orders for the last item can't both win.
  • F("stock") - quantity does the decrement in the database rather than in Python.
  • transaction.on_commit() sends the email only once the order really exists.
  • payments is passed in. In production it's a thin wrapper around your provider. In tests it's a fake. No mock.patch on a module path.
  • OutOfStock is a real exception. The caller decides what it means: a 409 for the API, a message in the admin, a log line in a batch job.

One honest caveat: charging a card inside a database transaction holds row locks while you wait on a network call. For a low-volume shop that's fine. At scale you'd split it into "reserve, then charge, then confirm" steps. The point is that once the logic lives in one function, that refactor is one file, not a hunt through serializers and signals.

The view and serializer get boring

class PlaceOrderInput(serializers.Serializer):
    items = LineInput(many=True)


class PlaceOrderView(APIView):
    permission_classes = [IsAuthenticated]

    def post(self, request):
        data = PlaceOrderInput(data=request.data)
        data.is_valid(raise_exception=True)
        lines = [LineRequest(**item) for item in data.validated_data["items"]]
        try:
            order = place_order(customer=request.user, lines=lines,
                                payments=get_payment_gateway())
        except OutOfStock as exc:
            return Response(
                {"error": "out_of_stock", "product_id": exc.product_id},
                status=status.HTTP_409_CONFLICT)
        return Response(OrderOutput(order).data,
                        status=status.HTTP_201_CREATED)

The serializer checks shape: is quantity an integer, is product_id present. The view maps HTTP to a call and exceptions to status codes. That's all either of them should ever do. Boring is the goal.

Testing without HTTP

Now the important rules are tested directly:

class FakePayments:
    def __init__(self, fail: bool = False) -> None:
        self.fail = fail
        self.charges: list[tuple[object, Decimal]] = []

    def charge(self, *, customer, amount: Decimal, reference: str) -> None:
        if self.fail:
            raise RuntimeError("card declined")
        self.charges.append((customer, amount))


def test_payment_failure_rolls_back_stock(db, customer, product_with_stock):
    product = product_with_stock(stock=3, price=Decimal("10.00"))

    with pytest.raises(RuntimeError):
        place_order(customer=customer,
                    lines=[LineRequest(product.pk, 2)],
                    payments=FakePayments(fail=True))

    product.refresh_from_db()
    assert product.stock == 3
    assert not Order.objects.exists()

No client, no JSON, no auth setup, no patching. The test reads like the rule it protects. Keep one or two API tests per endpoint to check the wiring, and put the volume of your tests at the service level.

Rules I actually follow

  • One use case, one function. place_order, cancel_order, refund_order. Name them after what the business says, not after HTTP verbs.
  • Keyword-only arguments. place_order(customer=..., lines=...) can't be called with arguments in the wrong order.
  • Services take values, not requests. Pass request.user, never request.
  • Reads can be selectors. A selectors.py with query functions keeps complex querysets out of views too. Simple Model.objects.filter() calls in a view are fine. Don't build ceremony for one-liners.
  • Models keep row-level logic. order.is_refundable() belongs on the model. "Refund this order, restock, notify the warehouse and reverse the charge" does not.
  • No signals for business flow. Signals are for decoupled side concerns like cache busting. If it's part of the use case, call it explicitly.
  • Don't build a framework. No abstract base Service class, no command bus, no dependency injection container. Functions and modules. Python already has them.

When this is overkill

A CRUD admin over a few tables doesn't need a service layer. If a ModelViewSet really is the whole feature, enjoy it. The moment an endpoint does more than save what it was given, such as touching a second model, calling an external API or enforcing a rule the business cares about, move it into a function. It takes ten minutes now, or a week later.

Bottom line

Django gives you an excellent ORM and a decent request cycle. It doesn't give you a place for your domain, so you have to make one. Thin views, dumb serializers, plain service functions. Your rules become callable from anywhere, testable in milliseconds and readable by the next developer, who is usually you, six months from now, at 11 pm, during an incident.

entry.title: The Problems with Django REST Framework
entry.summary: A critique of Django REST Framework: how it inherits Django Forms' design, its boilerplate and performance costs, the one thing it gets right, and why to move on.
entry.content:
Let's start by burying REST itself real quick, because DRF is built on the rotting foundation of a 2000s architectural cargo cult that's been wheezing since GraphQL, gRPC, tRPC, and even plain JSON-RPC started laughing at it.

RESTful, the idea was great in 2006 when Roy Fielding was drunk on HTTP verbs and everyone pretended HATEOAS was gonna save, decades later it's mostly a theater:

  • Over-fetching/under-fetching hell
  • N+1 query nightmares hidden behind "pagination"
  • Verb gymnastics for what should just be RPC calls
